title: Sukkot: Ecclesiastes
hookLine: Ecclesiastes, with its hard truths about time, is read in the season of joy
tomorrow: Sukkot: the season of our joy (Deuteronomy 16:14–15)

cards: The harvest is in. The sukkah is decorated. People are eating outside under the branches.
And on the Shabbat of Sukkot, in many synagogues, the reader chants a book that opens like this: "Vanity of vanities, saith Koheleth; vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Everything is fleeting.
What's the point of all your work? It sounds like the wrong book for the week. It was chosen on purpose.

teach.b: The book is Ecclesiastes. In Hebrew, Kohelet, the name its speaker gives himself; readers often take it as one who gathers, or one who speaks to a gathering.
He calls himself the son of David, king in Jerusalem, and tradition identifies him with King Solomon.
The word translated vanity, hevel, is the Hebrew word for breath, vapor. Not worthless, exactly. Fleeting, like breath on a cold morning: there, then gone.
Kohelet looks hard at life. You come into the world with nothing and leave with nothing. The wise die like fools.
You work, and someone else inherits it. There's nothing new under the sun.
And then: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." A time to be born, a time to die, a time to weep, a time to laugh. Why read this at Sukkot?
Several reasons are given. Sukkot is the harvest festival, when people feel richest and most secure, and Kohelet is a reminder not to mistake the barns for forever.
The sukkah teaches the same lesson: you leave your solid house to sit in a hut a wind could knock over. And Kohelet doesn't end in despair.
Again and again he comes back to joy: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart."
Enjoy life with the people you love, all the fleeting days. Joy isn't the opposite of knowing things pass. It may be the right response to it.
Sephardi communities generally don't read the book publicly; many Ashkenazi ones do.

how: In many Ashkenazi synagogues the book of Ecclesiastes (Kohelet) is read on the Shabbat during Sukkot, or on Shemini Atzeret when no Shabbat falls in the intermediate days; Sephardi communities generally do not read it publicly.

o: a scroll of a king's laws for his court
a song of praise sung after the harvest
Ecclesiastes, the book of fleeting breath

s: it means breath or vapor: fleeting, not worthless.
Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy.
every Jewish community reads Kohelet publicly on Sukkot

games.q: you're Kohelet. you've seen that wealth, wisdom and work all pass like breath. what's your advice?
o: eat your bread with joy, with the people you love.
games.why: Kohelet comes back again and again to joy: enjoy life in its fleeting days.

practice: Say one line of Ecclesiastes slowly, twice: a time to weep, and a time to laugh.

Then hold something good in your life that won't last forever, a child's age, a friendship in its easy season, the light this time of year, and let yourself enjoy it anyway, maybe more because of that.
If you pray, you can give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Kohelet. Ecclesiastes. The book of breath and fleeting things, read in the season of joy, which still tells you to eat your bread with joy.
